blocks.body:
Suppose a phone book holds a million names in alphabetical order and you want one particular name. Reading from the top could take a million looks. Opening at the middle, deciding which half the name is in, and repeating takes at most 20 looks. Both methods are correct; one is fifty thousand times faster in the worst case.

An algorithm is a recipe a machine could follow without judgement; its complexity counts the work it does as a function of the input size. With careful counting, recurrences and [[asymptotics|asymptotic notation]] one can predict running times, prove algorithms correct, and sometimes prove that no algorithm can do better.

blocks.title: What counts as an algorithm
blocks.body:
An algorithm takes an input from some specified set, performs a finite sequence of precisely defined steps, and stops with an output. Five properties are usually asked for: the input and output are specified; each step is unambiguous; each step can actually be carried out; the procedure always stops; and the output is correct for every valid input.

A first example: find the largest entry of a list $a_1, \dots, a_n$. Set $m = a_1$. For $i = 2, \dots, n$, if $a_i > m$, replace $m$ by $a_i$. Output $m$.

Why is this correct? Use a loop invariant: after the step for index $i$, the value $m$ is the largest of $a_1, \dots, a_i$. It holds after the start (with $i = 1$), and if it holds after step $i-1$ then step $i$ keeps it true, because the new $m$ is $\max(m, a_i)$. By [[induction]] it holds after step $n$, which is exactly the claim. Most correctness proofs for loops have this shape.

How much work does it do? Exactly $n - 1$ comparisons, whatever the input. Counting one kind of basic operation (comparisons, multiplications, array reads) and ignoring the rest is the standard simplification: it changes the true running time only by a constant factor, and constant factors depend on the machine anyway.

blocks.title: Worst-case time complexity
blocks.body:
Fix a notion of input size $n$ (the length of a list, the number of digits of a number, the number of vertices of a graph) and a basic operation. The worst-case time complexity of an algorithm is the function

$$T(n) = \max\{\text{number of basic operations on input } x : x \text{ has size } n\}.$$

The average-case complexity replaces the maximum by an average over a stated probability distribution on inputs of size $n$. In both cases we usually only record the growth rate, writing $T(n) = O(g(n))$ or $T(n) = \Theta(g(n))$.

In words: $T(n)$ is a guarantee. No input of size $n$ makes the algorithm do more than $T(n)$ basic steps.

blocks.title: Counting operations and growth rates
blocks.body:
Linear search looks for a target $t$ in a list by checking $a_1, a_2, \dots$ in turn. In the worst case (the target is last, or absent) it makes $n$ comparisons, so $T(n) = n$. If the target is present and equally likely to be in each position, the average is $(n+1)/2$: still linear.

Insertion sort builds a sorted list one item at a time, sliding each new item left past the larger items before it. If the input is in decreasing order, item number $k$ is compared with all $k - 1$ items before it, so the total is $1 + 2 + \cdots + (n-1) = n(n-1)/2$ comparisons. That is $\Theta(n^2)$.

Rounded values show why growth rate is what matters:

- $n = 10$: $\log_2 n \approx 3.3$, $n \log_2 n \approx 33$, $n^2 = 100$, $2^n = 1024$.
- $n = 1000$: $\log_2 n \approx 10$, $n \log_2 n \approx 9966$, $n^2 = 10^6$, $2^n \approx 1.07 \times 10^{301}$.
- $n = 10^6$: $\log_2 n \approx 19.9$, $n \log_2 n \approx 2.0 \times 10^7$, $n^2 = 10^{12}$.

An algorithm is called polynomial-time if $T(n) = O(n^k)$ for some fixed $k$, where $n$ is the length of the input written out in symbols. Exponential algorithms such as trying all $2^n$ subsets become hopeless around $n = 60$ or so.

blocks.title: Binary search
blocks.body:
Let $a_1 < a_2 < \cdots < a_n$ be sorted and let $t$ be a target. Binary search compares $t$ with the middle entry $a_m$, $m = \lfloor (1+n)/2 \rfloor$; it stops if $t = a_m$, and otherwise repeats on $a_1, \dots, a_{m-1}$ (if $t < a_m$) or on $a_{m+1}, \dots, a_n$ (if $t > a_m$), stopping with "absent" when the range is empty. In the worst case it makes exactly

$$C(n) = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + 1$$

three-way comparisons (each comparison decides $<$, $=$ or $>$), which is the number of binary digits of $n$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
After one comparison the two possible sub-ranges have $m - 1 = \lfloor (n-1)/2 \rfloor$ and $n - m = \lceil (n-1)/2 \rceil = \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ entries. The second is at least as large. An adversary can always answer so that the search continues in the larger range, and $C$ is nondecreasing (which follows from the recurrence below by strong induction), so with $C(0) = 0$,

$$C(n) = 1 + C(\lfloor n/2 \rfloor) \quad (n \ge 1).$$

Now let $b(n)$ be the number of binary digits of $n \ge 1$, with $b(0) = 0$. Deleting the last binary digit of $n$ gives $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$, so $b(n) = 1 + b(\lfloor n/2 \rfloor)$. The functions $C$ and $b$ satisfy the same recurrence with the same starting value, so by strong induction $C(n) = b(n)$ for all $n$. Finally, if $2^k \le n < 2^{k+1}$ then $n$ has $k + 1$ binary digits and $k = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$. For a million items this gives $C(10^6) = 20$.

blocks.title: Divide and conquer, and recurrences
blocks.body:
Merge sort splits a list of $n$ items into halves of sizes $\lceil n/2 \rceil$ and $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$, sorts each half recursively, then merges. Merging two sorted lists of lengths $p$ and $q$ is easy: repeatedly compare the two front items and move the smaller one to the output. Each comparison outputs one item, and when one list runs out the rest of the other is copied without comparisons, so at most $p + q - 1$ comparisons are needed. The worst-case number of comparisons therefore obeys

$$M(1) = 0, \qquad M(n) = M(\lceil n/2 \rceil) + M(\lfloor n/2 \rfloor) + n - 1.$$

For small $n$: $M(2) = 1$, $M(3) = 3$, $M(4) = 5$, $M(5) = 8$, $M(8) = 17$.

Many divide-and-conquer recurrences have the form $T(n) = a\,T(n/b) + f(n)$: split into $a$ subproblems of size $n/b$ and spend $f(n)$ on splitting and combining. Picture the recursion as a tree. Level $j$ has $a^j$ subproblems of size $n/b^j$, so if $f(n) = c\,n^d$ the work on level $j$ is $c\,n^d (a/b^d)^j$. This is a geometric series in $j$ with ratio $r = a/b^d$. If $r < 1$ the top level dominates, if $r = 1$ all $\log_b n$ levels contribute equally, and if $r > 1$ the bottom level (the $n^{\log_b a}$ leaves) dominates. This picture is the content of the next theorem.

blocks.title: Master theorem (polynomial case)
blocks.body:
Let $a \ge 1$, $b > 1$, $d \ge 0$ be constants and suppose $T(n) = a\,T(n/b) + \Theta(n^d)$, with $n/b$ read as $\lfloor n/b \rfloor$ or $\lceil n/b \rceil$. Then

$$T(n) = \begin{cases} \Theta(n^d) & \text{if } d > \log_b a,\\ \Theta(n^d \log n) & \text{if } d = \log_b a,\\ \Theta(n^{\log_b a}) & \text{if } d < \log_b a. \end{cases}$$

We do not prove the general statement here (the recursion-tree argument above is its proof sketch, and the rounding needs extra care; see Cormen et al.). The next result proves the merge sort case exactly when $n$ is a power of 2.

blocks.title: Comparisons in merge sort
blocks.body: For $n = 2^k$ with $k \ge 0$, the worst-case number of comparisons of merge sort is $M(n) = n \log_2 n - n + 1$. In particular $M(n) = \Theta(n \log n)$.

blocks.title: Lower bound for comparison sorting
blocks.body: Any algorithm that sorts $n$ distinct items using only comparisons between items makes at least $\lceil \log_2 n! \rceil$ comparisons on some input. Since $\log_2 n! \ge \frac{n}{2}\log_2 \frac{n}{2}$ for $n \ge 2$, this is $\Omega(n \log n)$, so merge sort is optimal up to a constant factor.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Run the algorithm on all $n!$ orderings of the items. Its behaviour is a binary decision tree: each internal node is a comparison "is $x < y$?", the two branches are the two answers, and each leaf is a final output. Two different orderings must reach different leaves, since the correct output (the permutation that sorts them) is different. So the tree has at least $n!$ leaves. A binary tree of height $h$ has at most $2^h$ leaves (induction on $h$), so $2^h \ge n!$ and the worst case $h$ satisfies $h \ge \log_2 n!$; as $h$ is an integer, $h \ge \lceil \log_2 n! \rceil$.

For the estimate: the largest $\lceil n/2 \rceil$ factors of $n!$ are each at least $n/2$, so $n! \ge (n/2)^{n/2}$ and $\log_2 n! \ge \frac{n}{2}\log_2\frac{n}{2}$.

For $n = 5$ the bound is $\lceil \log_2 120 \rceil = 7$. Merge sort uses $M(5) = 8$ in the worst case, so it is not exactly optimal for small $n$: cleverer schemes sort 5 items in 7 comparisons.

blocks.title: Dynamic programming
blocks.body:
Some recursions are slow because they solve the same subproblem many times. The Fibonacci numbers $F_0 = 0$, $F_1 = 1$, $F_n = F_{n-1} + F_{n-2}$ illustrate this. Computing $F_n$ by literally calling the definition makes $c(n)$ calls, where $c(0) = c(1) = 1$ and $c(n) = 1 + c(n-1) + c(n-2)$. One checks by induction that $c(n) = 2F_{n+1} - 1$, which grows like $1.618^n$: computing $F_{40}$ this way takes over 300 million calls. Yet there are only $n + 1$ different subproblems $F_0, \dots, F_n$. Computing them in increasing order and storing each answer takes $n - 1$ additions.

That is dynamic programming: identify a family of subproblems (stages and states), write the answer to each in terms of smaller ones (a recurrence, often called the Bellman equation in optimisation), and fill in a table from the smallest upward. The running time is roughly (number of states) times (work per state).

A typical decision problem: with coins of values 1, 3 and 4, what is the fewest coins summing to $n$? Let $g(n)$ be that number. The last coin used is 1, 3 or 4, so

$$g(0) = 0, \qquad g(n) = 1 + \min\{g(n-c) : c \in \{1,3,4\},\ c \le n\}.$$

The table for $n = 0, 1, \dots, 10$ is $0, 1, 2, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3$. Note $g(6) = 2$ (as $3 + 3$), while the greedy rule "always take the largest coin that fits" gives $4 + 1 + 1$, three coins.

blocks.title: Fast powers
blocks.body: Computing $x^n$ by multiplying $x$ by itself takes $n - 1$ multiplications. Show that $x^{13}$ can be computed with 5 multiplications, and that in general $x^n$ needs at most $2\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$ multiplications.
blocks.solution:
Write $13 = 1101_2 = 8 + 4 + 1$. Square repeatedly: $x^2 = x\cdot x$, $x^4 = x^2 \cdot x^2$, $x^8 = x^4\cdot x^4$ (3 multiplications). Then $x^{13} = x^8 \cdot x^4 \cdot x$ (2 more). Total 5, instead of 12. For $x = 3$ this gives $3^{13} = 1594323$.

In general let $k = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$, so $n$ has $k+1$ binary digits. Computing $x^{2}, x^{4}, \dots, x^{2^k}$ takes $k$ squarings. Then $x^n$ is the product of the powers $x^{2^j}$ for which digit $j$ of $n$ is 1; there are at most $k + 1$ of them, so at most $k$ further multiplications. The total is at most $2k$.

The same method computes $a^n \bmod N$ with numbers that never exceed $N^2$, in $O(\log n)$ multiplications. This is why [[rsa]] encryption with exponents hundreds of digits long is fast.

blocks.title: Solving recurrences
blocks.body: Find the growth rate of each: (a) $T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n$, (b) $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n^2$; and (c) $T(n) = 3T(n/2) + n$, the recurrence of Karatsuba's multiplication method for $n$-digit numbers.
blocks.solution:
(a) $a = 4$, $b = 2$, $\log_2 4 = 2 > d = 1$, so the leaves dominate: $\Theta(n^2)$.

(b) $\log_2 2 = 1 < d = 2$, so the top level dominates: $\Theta(n^2)$. The two recurrences have the same answer for opposite reasons.

(c) $\log_2 3 \approx 1.585 > 1$, so $T(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_2 3})$. Schoolbook multiplication of two $n$-digit numbers takes $\Theta(n^2)$ digit operations; Karatsuba's trick of replacing four half-size products by three gives a strictly smaller exponent.

blocks.title: The best block of consecutive days
blocks.body: A list of daily gains and losses $a_1, \dots, a_n$ is given (some negative). Find the largest possible sum of a block $a_i + a_{i+1} + \cdots + a_j$ of consecutive entries (at least one entry), in $O(n)$ time. Try it on $3, -4, 5, -1, 2, -6, 4$.
blocks.solution:
Checking all $\binom{n}{2} + n$ blocks is $\Theta(n^2)$ at best. Instead, let $E_j$ be the largest sum of a block that ends exactly at position $j$. Such a block is either $a_j$ alone or a best block ending at $j-1$ extended by $a_j$, so

$$E_1 = a_1, \qquad E_j = a_j + \max(E_{j-1}, 0).$$

The answer is $\max_j E_j$, since every block ends somewhere. One pass through the list computes all $E_j$ and their running maximum: $n - 1$ steps of constant work, so $\Theta(n)$.

Correctness is the invariant "after step $j$, the stored value equals $E_j$ and the running maximum equals the best block inside $a_1, \dots, a_j$", proved by induction on $j$ exactly as for the maximum-finding algorithm.

On the given list: $E = 3, -1, 5, 4, 6, 0, 4$, so the answer is 6, from the block $5 - 1 + 2$.

blocks.body:
- $O(g)$ is only an upper bound. Saying insertion sort is $O(n^3)$ is true but useless; use $\Theta$ when you mean the exact growth rate.
- Asymptotics hide constants. For lists of 10 items, insertion sort often beats merge sort in practice. Big-O predicts what happens as $n$ grows, not at every $n$.
- Input size means the length of the input. Trial division tests whether $N$ is prime with about $\sqrt{N}$ divisions. That looks polynomial, but $N$ has about $d = \log_{10} N$ digits, and $\sqrt{N} \approx 10^{d/2}$ is exponential in $d$. See [[primality]].
- A plausible greedy rule is not a proof. The coin example above shows the largest-coin rule failing.

The [[divisibility|Euclidean algorithm]] is one of the oldest algorithms and runs in $O(\log \min(a,b))$ division steps, which follows from the Fibonacci numbers being the worst case. Breadth-first search, Dijkstra's shortest paths and minimum spanning trees on [[graph-algorithms]] are analysed with the counting methods of this page; [[network-flows]] and [[linear-programming]] go further. Recurrences for running times are solved with the tools of [[sequences]] and [[generating-functions]]. Whether every problem whose solutions can be checked quickly can also be solved quickly is the [[p-vs-np]] question, and the security of [[rsa]] and [[discrete-log]] cryptography rests on believing some problems have no fast algorithm. At the extreme, [[computability]] shows that some problems have no algorithm at all.

1. Prove by induction that the number of calls $c(n)$ made by the naive Fibonacci recursion equals $2F_{n+1} - 1$.
2. Find the worst-case number of comparisons of merge sort for $n = 6$ and $n = 7$, and compare with $\lceil \log_2 n! \rceil$.
3. Use the master theorem to find the growth of $T(n) = 7T(n/2) + n^2$ (Strassen's matrix multiplication) and of $T(n) = 2T(n/4) + \sqrt{n}$.
4. With coins 1, 5 and 12, find the smallest amount for which the greedy rule does not give the fewest coins.
